query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating containerless levitation with fast differential scanning calorimetry and in-situ high-energy synchrotron/neutron radiography—after calibration on simpler systems—will enable accurate (±1–2% for Tm and ±3–5% for enthalpy and entropy) and efficient determination of melting-related thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy samples (e.g., equiatomic systems like CoCrCuNi and Al0.5CoCrFeNi) in their as-cast condition, representing fcc, bcc, and hcp crystal structures, prepared under controlled conditions ensuring homogeneous composition.
generation.intervention: Implement containerless processing (using electromagnetic or electrostatic levitation) integrated with FDSC and simultaneous in-situ high-energy synchrotron or neutron radiography. Begin with calibration experiments on simpler alloy systems to validate synchronization of temperature ramp, heat flow detection, and imaging.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under high-vacuum or inert atmosphere to prevent contamination. Samples are rapidly heated at rates between 10² and 10³ K/s from below the solidus to above the liquidus (up to approximately 2000 °C), with real-time imaging to capture morphology and volume change.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time high-energy radiography tracks liquid-phase morphology and density changes during melting, directly correlating the structural evolution with thermodynamic measurements from FDSC.
generation.mechanism: Containerless processing minimizes heterogeneous nucleation and heat loss while enabling rapid heating. FDSC precisely detects latent heat and melting transitions, whereas in-situ imaging directly quantifies volume changes, together providing intrinsic thermodynamic data by reducing artifacts typical in conventional DSC.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method is expected to yield melting temperatures with ±1–2% accuracy and enthalpy/entropy of fusion within ±3–5% accuracy, along with reliable liquid density and thermal expansion data. These measurements should be reproducible across diverse HEA compositions provided synchronization is effectively calibrated.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC techniques that are limited by container effects, thermal lag, and lack of direct structural observation, which typically result in larger uncertainties in measured melting properties.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to HEAs that are amenable to containerless processing and provide sufficient radiographic contrast. Challenges may arise with alloys having extreme melting points or compositions that reduce imaging contrast, which may require further methodological adjustments.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the degree of synchronization attainable under rapid heating, the extent to which calibration on simpler alloys will translate to complex HEAs, and potential limits in radiographic contrast for certain compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: First apply the integrated methodology on a simpler, well-characterized alloy system whose melting properties are well-established in the literature. After achieving accurate calibration (comparing FDSC and in-situ imaging data with conventional measurements), extend the method to a series of HEAs and compare the measured properties with CALPHAD predictions and independent DSC measurements.
measurements: Latent heat and phase transition peaks from FDSC
Volume change and liquid-phase density from real-time imaging
Calibration consistency across separate measurement techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the calibrated integrated approach yields melting temperatures or latent heat values deviating by more than 5% from benchmark measurements, or if synchronization between FDSC and imaging cannot be reliably established, then the proposed method is falsified.

A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. The field of high-entropy alloys continues to grow every year, and with this growth comes an enormous amount of never before seen alloy systems with unknown liquid state behavior. As previously shown, neutron imaging can be a very useful technique to elucidate the liquid state behavior of molten alloy systems. With the application of this technique to high-entropy alloys, in-situ imaging of liquid state miscibility has been observed for the first time with the equiatomic additions of Ni to the immiscible CoCrCu system. The current results show the following: Neutron imaging can be utilized to image liquid state behavior in high-entropy alloys. Imaging was carried out on equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with equiatomic additions of Ni such that when melting occurred between the alloying elements, full miscibility was achieved. In-situ neutron imaging was successfully utilized to image in-situ alloying of Ni into an immiscible CoCrCu system. The synthesis of the CoCrCuNi alloy inside the high-temperature furnace was fully imaged via a movie-like sequence of carefully timed radiographs to display the melting/alloying process. proposals.material_system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), for example, equiatomic systems such as CoCrCuNi and Al0.5CoCrFeNi, representative of fcc, bcc, and hcp crystal structures
proposals.intervention: Develop an integrated experiment that couples containerless processing (using electromagnetic or electrostatic levitation) with fast differential scanning calorimetry (FDSC) and in-situ high-energy synchrotron/neutron radiography
proposals.conditions: Samples are processed under high-vacuum or inert atmosphere to avoid contamination; heating rates in the range of 10²–10³ K/s from below the solidus to above the liquidus (typically up to 2000 °C depending on the alloy), with simultaneous radiographic imaging to capture morphology and volume change
proposals.structural_mediator: The liquid state morphology and density are tracked by high-energy radiography, serving as a structural indicator to directly correlate melting events with volumetric expansion or contraction
proposals.mechanism: Containerless processing minimizes heterogeneous nucleation and heat loss, while FDSC accurately captures latent heat signatures during melting. Simultaneous high-energy X-ray or neutron imaging quantifies real-time volume changes. Together, these measurements allow derivation of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties with reduced experimental uncertainties
proposals.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to achieve quantitative accuracies on the order of 1–2% for melting temperature, and 3–5% for enthalpy and entropy of fusion. Moreover, direct imaging of the volume change at melting will yield reliable liquid density and thermal expansion data. This combined method should efficiently apply across a broad range of HEA compositions, affording high-throughput, accurate property cataloging
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By integrating containerless levitation with rapid calorimetry and in-situ imaging, this strategy directly addresses the challenge of accurately and efficiently determining melting-related thermodynamic properties across different HEA families. It overcomes limitations associated with traditional DSC (such as container nucleation effects and thermal lag) and provides complementary structural evidence to ensure that the measured transition parameters truly reflect intrinsic material behavior

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposed integrated experiment directly targets the open question by measuring multiple melting-related thermodynamic properties (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change, and liquid-phase properties) simultaneously, thereby addressing limitations of traditional DSC methods.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system (various HEAs including fcc, bcc, and hcp variants) and operating conditions (containerless processing under high-vacuum/inert atmosphere, high heating rates up to 2000 °C) while ensuring that contamination and thermal lag are minimized.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; containerless processing minimizes heterogeneous nucleation and heat losses, FDSC accurately captures latent heat changes, and high-energy imaging provides real-time data on morphological and volumetric changes, which together yield intrinsic thermodynamic data.
critiques.feasibility: All individual components (electromagnetic/electrostatic levitation, FDSC, and in-situ high-energy synchrotron/neutron radiography) are established methods. However, their simultaneous integration may require careful synchronization and calibration, but it is feasible with current state-of-the-art equipment.
critiques.evidence: Supporting evidence comes from previous neutron imaging studies of HEAs (e.g., PMC8320920), where in-situ imaging was successfully used to observe liquid-phase behavior, and from established differential scanning calorimetry methods as detailed in several reports.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk lies in the experimental integration of multiple high-speed, high-temperature techniques in a containerless environment; synchronization and calibration between FDSC and in-situ radiography under rapid heating conditions could be challenging.
critiques.fix: Perform intermediate calibration experiments on simpler alloy systems to validate synchronization and data correlation between the levitation, FDSC, and imaging setups before applying the method across the full HEA family.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly tackles the challenge by integrating containerless processing, fast differential scanning calorimetry (FDSC), and in-situ high-energy radiography to measure melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties. The critic’s concerns regarding synchronization and calibration are addressable by incorporating intermediate calibration experiments on simpler alloy systems before applying the full method across the HEA family.
